name: Ruy López Berlin Endgame
summary: The Berlin Endgame (8.Qxd8+ Kxd8) is the queenless Berlin Wall where Black's bishop pair balances White's kingside pawn majority.
intro: The Berlin Endgame, the famous Berlin Wall, is reached by force after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nf6 4.O-O Nxe4 5.d4 Nd6 6.Bxc6 dxc6 7.dxe5 Nf5 8.Qxd8+ Kxd8, when the queens leave the board on move eight and a rich queenless struggle begins. Black emerges with the bishop pair and a solid if doubled c-pawn structure, but has surrendered the right to castle and must reroute a king stranded on d8. White, in return, holds a healthy kingside pawn majority and probes Black's displaced king and structure for the rest of the game. Renowned for its resilience and drawish reputation, the endgame shot to prominence when Vladimir Kramnik used it to neutralise Garry Kasparov in their 2000 World Championship match.
line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6 O-O Nxe4 d4 Nd6 Bxc6 dxc6 dxe5 Nf5 Qxd8+ Kxd8

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: The endgame is defined by the forcing sequence 4.O-O Nxe4 5.d4 Nd6 6.Bxc6 dxc6 7.dxe5 Nf5 8.Qxd8+ Kxd8, which trades the queens off very early and fixes the imbalance that governs everything after. Black owns the bishop pair but carries doubled c-pawns that cripple the nominal queenside majority, so it cannot easily manufacture a passed pawn. White, by contrast, keeps a clean four-against-three kingside majority that can roll forward to create a passer, the single most important long-term asset in the position.

The compensation for Black lies in the two bishops and the surprising safety of the king once the queens are gone. Although castling rights have been given up, the monarch is in little danger and instead becomes an asset, walking to c8 or e8 and beyond toward activity in the centre and queenside. White tries to advance the kingside majority, restrain the bishop pair with moves like h3 and knight regrouping, and exploit the awkward king, while Black leans on the bishops and precise coordination to hold. The balance of these factors gives the line its famously resilient, drawish character.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: White's main developing move is 9.Nc3, often followed by Rd1+ to harry the king and h3 to grant luft and prepare to blunt Black's light-squared bishop. Black's early decisions concern where to send the king, whether via ...Ke8 toward the kingside or ...Bd7 and ...Kc8 toward the queenside, how to develop the c8- and f8-bishops to squares like e6, d7, and e7, and where to reroute the f5-knight. Precise move orders matter, because a careless setup can let White's majority and initiative gather momentum.

Modern theory judges the endgame very solid for Black, and White's winning attempts are correspondingly subtle, built on the kingside majority and the small inconvenience of the displaced king rather than any concrete weakness. White may try plans with Ne2 and Ng3, b3 and a bishop on b2 or f4, and slow pressure on the e- and d-files, while Black aims to complete development, activate the bishops, and simplify toward drawn positions. Because the fortress is so hard to breach, many White players prefer to avoid it entirely with the Anti-Berlin 4.d3.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: Although the Berlin Defence itself dates to the nineteenth century, its specific queenless endgame long carried a mild reputation as slightly more comfortable for White, and for decades it was not a fashionable choice at the highest level. Deeper analysis gradually revealed how resourceful Black's position really is, with the bishop pair and king activity offsetting the structural and development concerns, and the assessment shifted toward full equality with best play.

The turning point came at the London 2000 World Championship match, where Kramnik adopted the Berlin Wall to blunt Kasparov's fearsome 1.e4, holding the endgame with such ease that the champion could never generate his customary pressure. That success set off an enormous revival, and the nickname Berlin Wall came to capture the line's near-impregnable defensive reputation. Its popularity at the elite level has since pushed a whole generation of White players toward sidestepping systems, above all the quiet 4.d3, in search of a livelier fight.

keyIdeas: The forcing line 8.Qxd8+ Kxd8 removes the queens very early.
Black gains the bishop pair but has doubled c-pawns and no castling.
White holds a healthy kingside pawn majority that can yield a passed pawn.
Black's king is safe without queens and walks to c8 or e8 for activity.
The line is famous for its resilient, drawish reputation.
Kramnik used it to neutralise Kasparov in their 2000 World Championship.

white: Advance the kingside pawn majority to create a passed pawn.
Restrain Black's bishop pair with h3, Nc3, and knight regrouping.
Use Rd1+ and rapid development to pressure the displaced king.
Fix and probe Black's crippled queenside with its doubled c-pawns.
Keep pieces on the board to exploit small king and structural edges.
black: Lean on the two bishops to control key diagonals and squares.
Walk the king to safety and activity via c8 and c7 or e8 and e7.
Blunt White's majority and neutralise the passed-pawn threat.
Develop harmoniously with ...Be7, ...Bd7 or ...Be6, and reroute the knight.
Simplify toward the line's drawish, fortress-like endgames.
